question.knowledge_point: Computing the Expected Value of a Scaled Random Variable
question.problem:
A random variable $X$ has the probability distribution given below.

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.35$ | $0.15$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ |

Calculate $\text{E}[-2X].$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's find $\text{E}[X].$ 

The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.35+1\cdot 0.15+2\cdot 0.15+3\cdot 0.1+4\cdot 0.25 \\  & =1.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[-2X] & =-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =-2\cdot 1.75 \\  & =-3.5.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Computing the Expected Value of a Scaled Random Variable

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Expected Value of a Transformed Random Variable
question.worked_solution:
For any constants $a$ and $b$ and any random variable $X,$ we have

$$
\text{E}[aX+b]=a\text{E}[X]+b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[-2X-4] & =-2\text{E}[X]-4 \\  & =-2(-\frac{5}{2})-4 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Computing the Expected Value of a Transformed Random Variable

question.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to Linear ODEs Using the Superposition Principle
question.problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\sqrt{x}$ are solutions to the equation $2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+3x{y}^{′}-y=0$ for $x>0,$ what function must also be a solution to the given differential equation?
question.worked_solution:
According to the superposition principle, if the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are solutions to a homogeneous, linear differential equation, and ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are constants, then $y(x)={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x)$ is also a solution to the equation.

We're given that ${y}_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore, the following function is also a solution:

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\frac{1}{x}+{c}_{2}\sqrt{x}
$$

If we let ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get:

$$
y(x)=\frac{2}{x}+\sqrt{x}=\frac{2+x\sqrt{x}}{x}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Parallel To a Straight Line Given Parametrically
question.problem:
Consider the straight line given by the following parametric equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-3+7t \\ y=5t \\ z=1-5t\end{aligned}
$$

Find a vector that is parallel to the line.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3+7t \\ 5t \\ 1-5t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7t \\ 5t \\ -5t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

This implies that the line passes through the point $(-3,0,1)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a Vector Parallel To a Straight Line Given Parametrically

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Line
question.problem: Find the parametric equations of the line that passes through the points $P(3,-3,5)$ and $Q(7,2,1).$
question.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ -4t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3+4t \\ -3+5t \\ 5-4t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ And finally, the parametric equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=3+4t \\ y=-3+5t \\ z=5-4t\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
question.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $3x.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3|x|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|3x|\sqrt{(3x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
question.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{6{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{6}}{|\sqrt{6}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{6}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{6}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{6}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{6{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{6}}{|\sqrt{6}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{6}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{6}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{6}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding Distributions of Squared Random Variables: Many-to-One Transformations
question.problem:
The random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution.

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.35$ | $0.15$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ |

Let $Y=16-{X}^{2}.$ The distribution of $Y$ is given below.

| $y$ | $0$ | $a$ | $16$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.35$ | $c$ | $d$ |

What is the value of $a+c?$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's add a $Y=16-{X}^{2}$ row to our table.

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $0$ | $15$ | $16$ | $15$ |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.35$ | $0.15$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ |

From the table, we see that $Y\in \{0,15,16\}.$ Notice that we now have two columns for $Y=15.$

We calculate the probabilities associated with each value of $Y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y=0) & =0.35 \\ P(Y=15) & =0.15+0.2 \\ P(Y=16) & =0.3\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following table.

| $y$ | $0$ | $15$ | $16$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.35$ | $0.35$ | $0.3$ |

Therefore, $a=15,c=0.35,$ and $a+c=15.35.$

question.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane
question.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=N\times R$ in the Cartesian plane?
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=N\times R
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in N,\,y\in R\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/067b3b386273b09d5614f934f6525bd3e43ff46f420eb8aa7e744f635ff6d101.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(2,y)\,:\,y\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/a870f65350ad00d258471079a34bec49a47d331c176dc7a91b3c7aae5ae968dd.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times N$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/c0df23ec47d729f597c02acff1530dd646a6f6c506a6497a8cb4d75b7fce5e74.png)

provenance.kp_title: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane

question.knowledge_point: Visualizing Unions of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
question.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=[-1,0]\times [-1,1]$ in the Cartesian plane?
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=[-1,0]\times [-1,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,0]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,0],\,y\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}=\{(0,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/c93f3ad399b88ccbaac990f8f73e93cfdcb1192f52b9b12f2d3ce178776fa13b.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in [-1,0]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}=\{(i,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,1]\}
$$

For each $i\in [-1,0],$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,-1)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/6557201d202a401a92ee37c9a69eab9ab6ab87c6342dbb9d2afebae30141346f.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I=[-1,0]:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/97a74b119ddb8a618d6564bc077d03a5a4ceb7152702beb3682f2eab1a436b70.png)
